title: Make a manual exception test fail for the right reason
summary: Trace a try/catch test, close its false-pass path, and preserve an exception when passing it onward.
goals: Explain why a missing exception can leave a manual test green.
Write a specific catch test with fail, a documented message check, and an unchanged-state check.
Distinguish rethrowing the same exception from wrapping it with a preserved cause.
setup: Continue Counter.set from lesson 20. We will read one path of a manual exception test at a time before assembling the method.

flow.title: Follow the expected exception into catch
flow.html:
Keep the same Counter: negative values are rejected. A manual exception test uses ordinary try and catch. If the call throws the named exception, Java skips the remaining statements in try and enters that catch block. Read this successful rejection path before checking the other path.

try {
    counter.set(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
}

flow.title: Trace the no-exception path
flow.html:
Now suppose a defect lets set(-1) return normally. The catch block is skipped. A test that contains an assertion only inside catch may reach its end without checking anything. That is a false pass: the test is green although the required rejection did not happen.

try {
    counter.set(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
}

flow.title: Close that path with fail
flow.html:
JUnit’s fail(message) immediately fails a test. Put it directly after the operation that must throw. A correct rejection jumps over it into catch. If the operation returns normally, execution reaches fail. The message explains which promised event was missing.

counter.set(-1);
fail("Expected a negative value to be rejected");

flow.title: Catch the promised type
flow.html:
The catch type is part of the check. A contract promising IllegalArgumentException is not satisfied by any arbitrary exception. Catching Exception can accidentally accept an unrelated runtime failure. A specific catch lets an unexpected type escape and make the test fail, which is useful evidence.

catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    // check this documented rejection
}

flow.title: Do not swallow the test’s own failure
flow.html:
Java’s Throwable is broader than Exception: it also includes errors. JUnit assertion failures are in the AssertionError family. A catch for Throwable can therefore catch your own fail call and hide it. Keep the catch focused on the production exception you expect.

try {
    counter.set(-1);
    fail("Expected rejection");
} catch (Throwable ex) {
    // accepts everything, including fail itself
}

flow.title: Check a message only when it is promised
flow.html:
An exception object can carry details. Use ex.getMessage() when the contract promises exact wording. Put that promised String first in assertEquals. Do not invent a message requirement from whatever the implementation happens to print; many contracts promise only a type.

assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());

flow.title: Rethrow the same exception
flow.html:
Production code may catch an exception briefly and then let its caller handle it. throw ex; rethrows the same object. It keeps the original exception type and details. Catching and silently returning would instead make the caller think the operation completed normally; choose that behavior only when it matches the contract.

catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    throw ex;
}

flow.title: Wrap a failure and keep its cause
flow.html:
Sometimes a wrapper has its own failure contract. It can translate a lower-level exception into another type while retaining the original as its cause. The two-argument constructor below takes a new context message and the caught exception. A one-argument message constructor would not keep that link automatically.

throw new IllegalStateException("Counter update failed", ex);

flow.title: Recognize the preserved object
flow.html:
getCause() returns the exception object that a wrapper retained. To check that it is the very same object, use assertSame. This is an identity question, unlike comparing two message Strings. A wrapper’s own message and its cause describe different layers of the failure.

IllegalArgumentException original =
    new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");
IllegalStateException wrapped =
    new IllegalStateException("Counter update failed", original);

flow.title: Assemble a complete manual test
flow.html:
Now combine the paths you have already checked. Arrange a valid object first. Put only the rejected action and the missing-exception failure in try. Catch the promised type, check its documented message, then observe state after the catch. The last assertion checks that rejection did not partly change the Counter.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(4);
// reject -1, then verify the value is still 4

practice.title: Follow the expected exception into catch
practice.prompt:
A valid counter must reject set(-1) with IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative"). The implementation does throw that exception. Which line checks its message?

try {
    counter.set(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
}
practice.hint: After the matching exception is thrown, execution enters catch.
practice.solution: The assertEquals line compares the documented text with the caught exception’s message.

options.feedback: This is the action that throws; it does not compare the message.
The expected text is first and the observed message is second.
This chooses the exception type to handle and names the caught object.

practice.title: Trace the no-exception path
practice.prompt:
The contract requires counter.set(-1) to throw IllegalArgumentException. A faulty version returns normally. This is the entire test body. What happens?

try {
    counter.set(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
}
practice.hint: Ask whether any assertion runs when the call returns normally.
practice.solution: The test reaches its end and passes without executing the assertion. It has no check on the missing-exception path.

options.text: It fails because catch was skipped.
options.feedback: Skipping catch is ordinary Java control flow; JUnit does not treat that as a failure.

options.text: It passes without checking the required rejection.
options.feedback: No exception and no failed assertion leave this test green.

options.text: It cannot compile because catch contains an assertion.
options.feedback: An assertion call is legal inside catch.

practice.title: Close that path with fail
practice.prompt:
A valid counter must reject set(-1) with IllegalArgumentException. Write the single missing JUnit statement so this test fails when the call returns normally. Assume assertion imports are present.

try {
    counter.set(-1);
    // missing statement
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
}
practice.hint: Use fail with a message describing the missing exception.
practice.solution:
fail("Expected a negative value to be rejected");

This statement belongs inside try, immediately after the call.
rubric: Calls JUnit fail(...), rather than printing a message.
Places it after set(-1) inside try.
Uses a clear message and ends the statement with a semicolon.

practice.title: Catch the promised type
practice.prompt: The contract promises IllegalArgumentException for counter.set(-1). A defect instead throws NullPointerException. Which catch clause avoids accepting that wrong type as success? The catch body would otherwise simply return.
practice.hint: Choose the promised exception family, not every Exception.
practice.solution: catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) does not catch NullPointerException. The unexpected exception escapes and the test fails.

options.feedback: Both exception types are Exceptions, so this would also accept the wrong one.
It catches the required family without swallowing the unrelated NullPointerException.
That accepts the observed defect instead of checking the promised rejection.

practice.title: Do not swallow the test’s own failure
practice.prompt:
The required exception from counter.set(-1) is IllegalArgumentException. In this test, suppose set returns normally. Explain in two sentences why the test can still pass and name the catch type that repairs this particular problem.

try {
    counter.set(-1);
    fail("Expected rejection");
} catch (Throwable ex) {
}
practice.hint: fail throws an assertion failure, which is also a Throwable.
practice.solution: The call returns normally, so fail throws a JUnit assertion failure; the broad Throwable catch swallows that failure. Catch IllegalArgumentException instead so the test’s own assertion failure escapes.
rubric: Traces the normal return into fail.
Explains that catch(Throwable) catches the assertion failure.
Names IllegalArgumentException as the promised catch type.

practice.title: Check a message only when it is promised
practice.prompt: Inside catch (IllegalArgumentException ex), verify the documented exact message "value must be nonnegative". Write one Jupiter assertion. Assume assertion imports are present.
practice.hint: The expected String is the first argument; the caught exception supplies the actual String.
practice.solution: assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
rubric: Uses assertEquals with two String values.
Puts the documented message first.
Reads the actual message using ex.getMessage() and ends with a semicolon.

practice.title: Rethrow the same exception
practice.prompt: A wrapper method promises to let the original IllegalArgumentException reach its caller. It has already caught that exception in a variable named ex. Which statement rethrows that same object?
practice.hint: Use throw followed by the existing exception variable.
practice.solution: throw ex; sends the same caught object onward. It does not construct a replacement exception.

options.feedback: Returning normally hides the failure from the caller.
This creates another exception and loses the original message and cause information.
This rethrows the existing exception object.

practice.title: Wrap a failure and keep its cause
practice.prompt: A wrapper catches IllegalArgumentException ex from counter.set(value). Its own contract requires IllegalStateException with message "Counter update failed", preserving ex as the cause. Write the throw statement.
practice.hint: Use the constructor with both a message and a Throwable cause.
practice.solution: throw new IllegalStateException("Counter update failed", ex);
rubric: Throws a new IllegalStateException.
Supplies the exact wrapper message.
Passes the existing ex as the second constructor argument.

practice.title: Recognize the preserved object
practice.prompt:
Which assertion verifies that the wrapper preserved the original exception object as its cause? Assume Jupiter assertion imports.

IllegalArgumentException original =
    new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");
IllegalStateException wrapped =
    new IllegalStateException("Counter update failed", original);
practice.hint: The requirement says same object, not same message.
practice.solution: assertSame(original, wrapped.getCause());

options.feedback: getCause returns the retained object, and assertSame checks identity.
The two layers intentionally have different messages.
That would require the cause to be absent.

practice.title: Assemble a complete manual test
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

Assume the Jupiter @Test and assertion imports are present. Write the method inside an ordinary test class.

Write void negativeSetLeavesValue() as a complete @Test method using manual try/catch. Start at 4, attempt -1, fail if nothing is thrown, check the exact message, and check that the value is still 4.
practice.hint: Arrange outside try; fail immediately after set(-1); use a specific catch; check get() afterward.
practice.solution:
@Test
void negativeSetLeavesValue() {
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    counter.set(4);
    try {
        counter.set(-1);
        fail("Expected a negative value to be rejected");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
    }
    assertEquals(4, counter.get());
}

An unexpected exception escapes; a missing exception reaches fail. This method checks both the rejection details and the unchanged state.
rubric: Uses @Test and a non-private, non-static void method with no parameters.
Creates a fresh Counter and stores 4 before try.
Calls set(-1), then fail, inside try.
Catches IllegalArgumentException and checks the documented message expected-first.
Checks assertEquals(4, counter.get()) after the catch.

bridge: You can now tell whether a test really checks rejection. Next, place the production guards that make that rejection reliable.

title: Put a guard before the operation it protects
summary: Translate input rules into guards, preserve state on rejection, and distinguish Java assert from JUnit assertions.
goals: Place null, range, and state guards before dependent work.
Test one invalid obligation at a time without inventing exception priority.
Explain why public input validation must not depend on Java assert.
setup: Continue Counter.set, then transfer the same guard-before-use rule to an array index.

flow.title: Translate the invalid region
flow.html:
A guard checks a condition before the main work. Counter accepts zero and positive values, so its invalid region is strictly below zero. Write the guard from that rule, not from a single example. The exception message is part of this Counter’s stated contract.

if (next < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");
}

flow.title: Validate before changing state
flow.html:
Rejecting an input is not enough if the object has already been changed. Counter promises to keep its old value on rejection. The guard must run before assigning to the field. Read statements in execution order: once an assignment has executed, throwing an exception does not automatically undo it.

if (next < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");
}
value = next;

flow.title: Check the accepted edge too
flow.html:
A rejection test can pass even when a guard rejects too much. After testing a negative input, check the neighboring valid boundary. For Counter that boundary is zero. Because set returns void, call it as a statement and then inspect get. A thrown exception will fail this ordinary acceptance test.

counter.set(0);
assertEquals(0, counter.get());

flow.title: Guard a reference before dereferencing it
flow.html:
Transfer the same ordering rule to an array. Reading values.length needs an actual array object. If values is null, that read fails before a later guard can help. A null check therefore comes before using length or an element. The chosen exception type still comes from the method’s contract.

if (values == null) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("values required");
}
int count = values.length;

flow.title: Read short-circuit protection in order
flow.html:
Short-circuit Boolean operators also have an order. With ||, Java skips the right side when the left side is true. That makes the null check below protect the length check. Swapping the two tests removes the protection for null. Use the combined form only when both invalid inputs have the same contracted response.

if (values == null || values.length == 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("values required");
}

flow.title: Guard both ends of an index range
flow.html:
An array of length three has indexes 0, 1, and 2. A valid index is at least zero and less than the array length. A rejection guard checks the opposite: below zero or at least length. The null guard must already have succeeded before this range guard reads length.

if (index < 0 || index >= values.length) {
    throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException("index outside array");
}

flow.title: Isolate one invalid obligation
flow.html:
A test with several invalid arguments may fail before reaching the rule you wanted to check. To test an index guard, provide a non-null array. To test a null guard, avoid claiming which other rule should win unless the contract specifies priority. Isolation makes the exception’s source easier to interpret.

ArrayRules.at(new int[]{7}, -1);

flow.title: Do not make validation optional
flow.html:
Java has a language statement named assert. It can check an internal assumption, but it is normally disabled unless assertions are enabled for that code. Public input validation must still work when it is disabled. Keep required rejection in ordinary if/throw code that always executes.

assert next >= 0; // not a reliable public-input guard

flow.title: Separate the three kinds of check
flow.html:
The names sound similar but the roles differ. An ordinary guard enforces a production contract. Java assert checks an internal assumption when enabled. A Jupiter assertion such as assertEquals checks a test’s expectation when that test runs. Turning off Java assertions does not turn off JUnit’s assertion methods.

assertEquals(0, counter.get()); // a Jupiter test assertion

flow.title: Test rejection and preservation together
flow.html:
A guard test can check two promised effects of one rejected action: the exception and the unchanged state. Establish the state before the exception assertion. Keep the lambda limited to the rejected call. Read the stored value afterward; this detects a guard that throws only after mutating the field.

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
    () -> counter.set(-1));
assertEquals(4, counter.get());

practice.title: Translate the invalid region
practice.prompt: void Counter.set(int next) must accept every nonnegative integer and reject every negative integer. Which condition belongs in the rejection guard?
practice.hint: Zero is valid. The guard should be true only for negative values.
practice.solution: next < 0 identifies exactly the invalid region.

options.feedback: This wrongly rejects the valid boundary value zero.
This rejects negatives while allowing zero and positives.
This misses other negative values such as -2.

practice.title: Validate before changing state
practice.prompt:
The field int value currently stores 4. set(int next) must reject negatives and preserve the old field. Reorder these statements into a correct method body; do not change the contract.

value = next;
if (next < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");
}
practice.hint: The assignment must be unreachable when the guard throws.
practice.solution:
if (next < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");
}
value = next;
rubric: Places the negative guard before value = next.
Keeps next < 0 so zero remains accepted.
Throws the promised IllegalArgumentException and retains the assignment for valid inputs.

practice.title: Check the accepted edge too
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

A fresh Counter counter = new Counter(); has been created, and it then received counter.set(4);. Write the two statements that verify zero is accepted and stored. Jupiter assertions are imported.
practice.hint: Perform the void call first, then compare the observed state.
practice.solution:
counter.set(0);
assertEquals(0, counter.get());
rubric: Calls counter.set(0) as a separate statement.
Checks counter.get() against expected 0.
Does not try to use the void call as an assertion argument.

practice.title: Guard a reference before dereferencing it
practice.prompt: static int ArrayRules.count(int[] values) promises IllegalArgumentException("values required") for null. Which first statement permits that deliberate rejection before any array access?
practice.hint: Do not evaluate values.length until the reference has passed the null guard.
practice.solution: The explicit null guard can throw the contracted exception before any dereference occurs.

options.feedback: For null this dereferences the reference and throws NullPointerException first.

options.text: if (values == null) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("values required"); }
options.feedback: This checks the reference itself without using the absent object.
This dereferences the reference and also assumes an element exists.

practice.title: Read short-circuit protection in order
practice.prompt:
A method promises the same IllegalArgumentException for null and empty arrays. In the condition below, what happens when values is null?

values == null || values.length == 0
practice.hint: For ||, a true left side already determines the result.
practice.solution: The left side is true, so Java does not evaluate values.length. The complete condition is true without a null dereference.

options.text: It evaluates length and throws NullPointerException.
options.feedback: The right side is skipped because the left side is true.

options.text: It is true, and values.length is not evaluated.
options.feedback: This is the protection supplied by left-to-right short circuit evaluation.

options.text: It is false because null is not an empty array.
options.feedback: Null and empty differ, but the left alternative explicitly recognizes null.

practice.title: Guard both ends of an index range
practice.prompt: static int ArrayRules.at(int[] values, int index) has already rejected null. It must reject indexes below 0 or at least values.length with IndexOutOfBoundsException("index outside array"). Write the if guard, before return values[index];.
practice.hint: Join the two invalid regions with ||, not &&.
practice.solution:
if (index < 0 || index >= values.length) {
    throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException("index outside array");
}
rubric: Uses index < 0 for the lower invalid region.
Uses index >= values.length for the upper invalid region.
Joins them with || and throws the specified exception before indexing.

practice.title: Isolate one invalid obligation
practice.prompt: static int ArrayRules.at(int[] values, int index) rejects null with IllegalArgumentException and an out-of-range index with IndexOutOfBoundsException. Priority for two invalid arguments is unspecified. Which call cleanly tests the negative-index rule?
practice.hint: Keep values valid while making only index invalid.
practice.solution: at(new int[]{7}, -1) isolates an invalid index with an otherwise usable one-element array.

options.feedback: Both arguments are invalid; the contract does not state which rejection takes priority.
Only the index violates its requirement.
This is a valid call that should return 7.

practice.title: Do not make validation optional
practice.prompt:
A public Counter.set(int next) must always reject negatives. Its body is shown below. Java language assertions are disabled. What does set(-1) do?

assert next >= 0;
value = next;
practice.hint: A disabled Java assert statement performs no check.
practice.solution: The assert statement is skipped and the field receives -1, violating the public contract.

options.feedback: Java assert does not express that required exception, and it is disabled here.

options.text: Stores -1 because the assert check is disabled.
options.feedback: The assignment still executes.

options.text: Cannot compile because assert is only available in JUnit.
options.feedback: assert is a Java keyword, separate from JUnit assertion methods.

practice.title: Separate the three kinds of check
practice.prompt: Select all accurate statements about production guards, Java language assert, and JUnit Jupiter assertion methods.
practice.hint: Separate an always-executed if statement from an optional language assertion and a test-library call.
practice.solution: An ordinary if/throw guard enforces the required input rule. Jupiter assertions continue to work when Java language assertions are disabled.

options.text: Use if/throw for a public rejection that must always happen.
options.feedback: This check does not depend on enabling Java assertions.

options.text: Disabling Java assert also disables assertEquals.
options.feedback: assertEquals is an ordinary method supplied by JUnit, not the assert keyword.

options.text: JUnit assertions compare test expectations when the test runs.
options.feedback: Their role is checking behavior in tests.

options.text: Java assert is the correct way to guarantee a public IllegalArgumentException.
options.feedback: It can be disabled and, when false and enabled, raises AssertionError instead.

practice.title: Test rejection and preservation together
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

Assume the Jupiter @Test and assertion imports are present. Write the method inside an ordinary test class.

Write void negativeSetDoesNotMutate(). Arrange value 4, call set with -1 inside assertThrows, and verify the value remains 4. No message assertion is required in this exercise.
practice.hint: The setup is outside the lambda, and the state check is after assertThrows.
practice.solution:
@Test
void negativeSetDoesNotMutate() {
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    counter.set(4);
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
        () -> counter.set(-1));
    assertEquals(4, counter.get());
}
rubric: Uses a valid @Test void method and a fresh Counter.
Sets 4 before the checked action.
Uses IllegalArgumentException.class and a lambda containing only set(-1).
Checks expected 4 against counter.get() after the rejection.

bridge: You can now connect a guard to its contract. Next, trace faulty code and choose a concrete input that exposes the defect.

title: Explain a defect with an input that reveals it
summary: Read a small search method, distinguish compile failures from runtime behavior, and turn a trace into a regression test.
goals: Choose a concrete witness that reaches and exposes a defect.
Distinguish type errors, early returns, off-by-one bounds, and wrong Boolean expressions.
Explain expected behavior, actual behavior, and the faulty statement separately.
setup: We move from Counter guards to a tiny array search. Its contract supplies the expected answer before we inspect each implementation.

flow.title: Read the search result type
flow.html:
Return to firstIndex, the left-to-right search introduced earlier. Its int result is an index, with -1 meaning no match. The return type rules out returning null. Check whether a method can compile before trying to explain what it does at runtime.

static int firstIndex(int[] values, int target) {
    return null;
}

flow.title: Set the expected result before tracing
flow.html:
The contract is your independent source of expected behavior. For a first match, count array indexes from zero and stop at the earliest matching element. Repeated values matter: returning any matching index is weaker than returning the first. Establish that expected index before looking at a suspicious loop.

int[] values = new int[]{4, 9, 9};
// Searching for 9 must return index 1.

flow.title: Trace an early return
flow.html:
A return exits the entire method, not just the current loop iteration. In this faulty version, the no-match return is inside the loop. After a first-element mismatch, execution stops before examining later elements. Trace one input one statement at a time instead of guessing from the method’s name.

for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
    if (values[i] == target) {
        return i;
    }
    return -1;
}
return -1;

flow.title: Choose an exposing witness
flow.html:
A witness is a concrete input that demonstrates a mismatch. Merely executing a faulty line is not enough; its effect must become visible. The early-return search needs a first mismatch followed by a later match. A first-element match can make this defective method look correct.

Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{4, 9}, 9); // reveals it

flow.title: Repair the return’s location
flow.html:
A search can conclude “absent” only after exhausting all candidates. Keep the successful return inside the matching branch, but put the final no-match return after the loop. Moving a statement can change which evidence is available when it executes, even though the returned value itself stays the same.

for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
    if (values[i] == target) {
        return i;
    }
}
return -1;

flow.title: Expose an off-by-one bound
flow.html:
Now inspect a different faulty version. An array’s largest valid index is length minus one. Using <= length allows one extra iteration. An empty array is a small witness: its length is zero, so the faulty loop tries index zero immediately. This is a runtime indexing failure, not a compilation failure.

for (int i = 0; i <= values.length; i++) {
    if (values[i] == target) {
        return i;
    }
}
return -1;

flow.title: Distinguish assignment from comparison
flow.html:
One character can change both meaning and type. == compares two ints and produces a boolean. = assigns an int and has an int value. Java requires a boolean condition in if, so an int assignment in that position is a compile error. Do not describe it as a wrong runtime branch.

if (values[i] = target) {
    return i;
}

flow.title: Turn the witness into an assertion
flow.html:
Once the contract and trace disagree, preserve that input as a test. The expected value comes from the contract, even while the current implementation returns something else. This assertion stays red until the early-return defect is corrected; changing the expected value to match the defect would erase the evidence.

assertEquals(1, Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{4, 9}, 9));

flow.title: Give the witness its own test method
flow.html:
A named test makes the purpose of the witness visible in a test report. The method name can describe the missed behavior: finding a match after an initial mismatch. Use the same assertion you just built inside a complete @Test method. No exception assertion belongs in this ordinary successful-search case.

@Test
void findsMatchAfterFirstMismatch() {
    assertEquals(1, Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{4, 9}, 9));
}

flow.title: Explain the mechanism precisely
flow.html:
A useful explanation connects three facts: what the contract requires, what this execution does, and which statement causes the difference. “The loop is broken” does not supply that connection. Keep the explanation specific enough that another reader can trace the same witness without guessing your input or expected result.

For {4, 9} searching for 9: expected 1; actual -1; the return after the first mismatch prevents a second iteration.

flow.title: Recognize integer division before the return conversion
flow.html:
Transfer the same expected-versus-actual reading to a tiny arithmetic method. With two int operands, division discards the fractional part. Returning that int result from a double method converts the already-truncated number; it does not recover the fraction. A contract promising an exact half therefore needs a different arithmetic expression for odd inputs.

static double half(int value) {
    return value / 2;
}

flow.title: Make one division operand a double
flow.html:
A decimal literal such as 2.0 is a double value. When one operand is double, this division uses floating-point arithmetic: 5.0 / 2 and 5 / 2.0 both produce 2.5. The repair belongs in the expression, before the fraction can be lost. An odd-number witness is needed because an even input can conceal truncation.

return value / 2.0;

flow.title: Use nonzero state to expose addition instead of replacement
flow.html:
Return to Counter for a stateful witness. A faulty setter using value += next can look correct when value starts at zero: zero plus five is five. Set a nonzero value first, then replace it. The setup makes the difference between addition and replacement visible in the final observation.

counter.set(4);
counter.set(5); // expected 5, but += produces 9

practice.title: Read the search result type
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

Classify this implementation before attempting to run it.

static int firstIndex(int[] values, int target) {
    return null;
}
practice.hint: int is a primitive type and cannot hold null.
practice.solution: This is a compile-time type error: the declared primitive int result cannot be null. There is no runtime return value to trace.

options.feedback: Java does not convert null into the no-match sentinel -1.

options.text: It fails to compile because null is not an int.
options.feedback: The returned expression is incompatible with the primitive result type.

options.text: It compiles, then throws when the array is empty.
options.feedback: Compilation fails before any input can be executed.

practice.title: Set the expected result before tracing
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

For new int[]{7, 3, 7} and target 7, what is the expected result?
practice.hint: The first element has index zero.
practice.solution: The first 7 is at index 0. A later match does not change the required first-match result.

options.feedback: The element at index zero is already the first match.
That is a matching index, but not the first one.
The method returns an index, not the matching value.

practice.title: Trace an early return
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

For values new int[]{4, 9} and target 9, what does this faulty body actually return?

for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
    if (values[i] == target) {
        return i;
    }
    return -1;
}
return -1;
practice.hint: At i = 0, 4 does not equal 9. Which statement executes next?
practice.solution: It returns -1 immediately after the first mismatch. The expected result is 1, but index 1 is never examined.

options.feedback: That is the expected result, but the early return prevents the second iteration.
The first mismatch reaches the return inside the loop.
It terminates too soon, at the first iteration.

practice.title: Choose an exposing witness
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

A faulty implementation returns -1 immediately after its first mismatching element; otherwise it returns the matching index, or -1 for an empty array. Select every call that exposes this specific defect.
practice.hint: Look for a first mismatch and a match later in the array.
practice.solution: The arrays {4, 9} and {2, 3, 9} both require searching past an initial mismatch to find 9.

options.feedback: Expected 1, but the faulty method returns -1 after inspecting 4.
The first element matches, so this method returns the correct index 0.
Expected 2, but the first mismatch incorrectly ends the search.
Both the correct and faulty versions return -1 for this empty case.

practice.title: Repair the return’s location
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

Repair the method below by removing the incorrectly placed return. Keep a valid return for an empty array and an exhausted search.

static int firstIndex(int[] values, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
        return -1;
    }
    return -1;
}
practice.hint: The failed search result belongs after the loop.
practice.solution:
static int firstIndex(int[] values, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
rubric: Removes the return -1 inside the loop.
Keeps return i only for a matching element.
Keeps return -1 after the loop, including the empty-array path.

practice.title: Expose an off-by-one bound
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

The body below receives an empty non-null array and target 9. What is the observed failure?

for (int i = 0; i <= values.length; i++) {
    if (values[i] == target) {
        return i;
    }
}
return -1;
practice.hint: For length zero, 0 <= 0 is true, but index zero does not exist.
practice.solution: The first array access throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; the contract expected -1. Change the loop bound to i < values.length.

options.text: A compile error because <= is not allowed in a loop.
options.feedback: The comparison is legal Java; it expresses the wrong bound.
The empty array has no valid indexes, but the loop body executes.
The exception occurs before execution can reach the final return.

practice.title: Distinguish assignment from comparison
practice.prompt:
values is int[], and i and target are ints. Explain why the following condition does not compile, then give the corrected if header for an equality check.

if (values[i] = target) {
    return i;
}
practice.hint: The expression after a single = is an int here; if needs boolean.
practice.solution:
A single = assigns target to an int array element, producing an int expression rather than a boolean. Use the equality comparison:

if (values[i] == target) {
rubric: Identifies assignment with = rather than equality comparison.
Explains the int-versus-boolean compile-time mismatch.
Gives values[i] == target as the corrected condition.

practice.title: Turn the witness into an assertion
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

Write one Jupiter assertion for the revealing input new int[]{4, 9}, target 9. A faulty implementation currently returns -1; the assertion must preserve the contractual expectation. Assertion imports are present.
practice.hint: Index 1 contains the first 9. Put that expected index first.
practice.solution: assertEquals(1, Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{4, 9}, 9));
rubric: Uses expected 1, derived from the first-match contract.
Calls Searches.firstIndex with the stated int[] and int.
Uses assertEquals(expected, actual) and a semicolon.

practice.title: Give the witness its own test method
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

Assume the Jupiter @Test and assertion imports are present. Write the method inside an ordinary test class.

Write a complete test method named findsLastPosition() for values new int[]{2, 4, 9} and target 9.
practice.hint: The third element has index 2. The method returns an int normally.
practice.solution:
@Test
void findsLastPosition() {
    assertEquals(2, Searches.firstIndex(new int[]{2, 4, 9}, 9));
}
rubric: Uses @Test with void findsLastPosition() and a body.
Passes the supplied array and target.
Checks expected index 2 with assertEquals.

practice.title: Explain the mechanism precisely
practice.prompt:
static int Searches.firstIndex(int[] values, int target) accepts a non-null array. It returns the first matching index, or -1 if no element matches. An empty array has no match.

Explain the defect for input new int[]{4, 9}, target 9, using expected result, actual result, and cause. This is the complete faulty body:

for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
    if (values[i] == target) {
        return i;
    }
    return -1;
}
return -1;
practice.hint: Trace i = 0, then identify the statement that prevents i = 1.
practice.solution: The first matching 9 is at index 1, so the expected result is 1. The implementation returns -1 after comparing 4 with 9 at index 0. Its no-match return is inside the loop, so it exits before checking index 1; move that return after the loop.
rubric: States the exact input and expected index 1.
States actual return -1.
Connects the early return inside the loop to the skipped later match.
Does not call this a compile error or claim every input fails.

practice.title: Recognize integer division before the return conversion
practice.prompt:
static double Numbers.half(int value) promises the mathematical half, including a fractional part. What does the implementation below actually return for value 5?

static double half(int value) {
    return value / 2;
}
practice.hint: Both division operands are ints, so 5 / 2 is computed before conversion to double.
practice.solution: It returns 2.0, although the contract expects 2.5. Integer division first produces 2, which is then converted to double.

options.text: 2.5, because the method’s result type is double.
options.feedback: The result type does not change the operand types of the preceding division.

options.text: 2.0, because integer division discards the fraction first.
options.feedback: The truncation occurs before the return conversion.

options.text: It cannot compile because int results can never be converted to double.
options.feedback: The widening conversion is legal; the defect is the lost fractional value.

practice.title: Make one division operand a double
practice.prompt:
static double Numbers.half(int value) promises the mathematical half, including fractions. Replace the faulty return statement with one that preserves the half of odd int inputs. Then name one revealing input and its expected result.

return value / 2;
practice.hint: Use the double divisor 2.0; input 5 should produce 2.5.
practice.solution:
return value / 2.0;

For value 5, expected 2.5. This odd input distinguishes the repaired expression from the old integer division, which returned 2.0.
rubric: Uses double division before any truncation, for example value / 2.0.
Retains the method’s half operation rather than hard-coding one result.
Gives an odd input and its correct fractional expected value.

practice.title: Use nonzero state to expose addition instead of replacement
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

For valid inputs a faulty setter executes value += next;. Which fresh-Counter sequence exposes that error with an expected value different from the actual value?
practice.hint: Begin the target replacement from a nonzero stored value.
practice.solution: Set 4, then set 5, then read get: expected 5, actual 9. A single set from zero can hide this addition defect.

options.text: Create Counter; set(5); expect get() to be 5.
options.feedback: The faulty implementation also gives 5 because it adds to initial zero.

options.text: Create Counter; set(4); set(5); expect get() to be 5.
options.feedback: The faulty implementation adds 4 and 5, revealing actual 9.

options.text: Create Counter; set(0); expect get() to be 0.
options.feedback: Both assignment and addition leave initial zero unchanged here.

bridge: A revealing input gives you evidence for a defect. Next, use operation sequences to expose inconsistent object state.

title: Keep the stored structure consistent
summary: Follow empty, singleton, and longer queue states, then distinguish a copied reference from independent contents.
goals: Connect a representation invariant to a concrete queue state.
Test zero, one, many, and reuse sequences through the queue API.
Use mutation to distinguish aliasing, array copies, and shallow object copies.
setup: Return to the FIFO queue idea from lesson 14. Its public behavior stays the same while we inspect how a linked representation can become inconsistent.

flow.title: Begin with the queue’s public rule
flow.html:
Return to a queue: the first value added is the first removed. We will use a small IntQueue whose methods accept and return ints. The public rule comes first because it supplies expected behavior even if you do not know the representation. Adding 4 and then 9 must make 4 the next removal.

IntQueue queue = new IntQueue();
queue.add(4);
queue.add(9);

flow.title: Name the representation’s links
flow.html:
A linked queue stores each value in a node. A node’s next field refers to the following node; null marks the end. The queue’s head points to the first node and tail to the last. These are references to nodes, not indexes into an array.

Node head;
Node tail;
int size;

flow.title: Count reachable nodes
flow.html:
A representation invariant is a rule that must hold for every valid stored state. One queue invariant says size equals the number of nodes reached by following next from head. It connects a summary field to the structure it summarizes. A method can return a plausible value while leaving this rule broken.

If following next from head visits two nodes and then null, the stored size must be 2.

flow.title: Represent the empty state consistently
flow.html:
For this linked queue, an empty state has size zero and both endpoints null. With nodes present, tail must name the final reachable node and its next must be null. Each clause checks a different relationship. Checking only size == 0 can miss an endpoint left pointing at a removed node.

size == 0 && head == null && tail == null

flow.title: Repair the last-removal transition
flow.html:
A singleton removal is special because removing head also removes the last node. After advancing head to null, clear tail too. Do not clear tail after every removal: when nodes remain, it still identifies their last node. The condition should follow the new state of head.

head = head.next;
size--;
if (head == null) {
    tail = null;
}

flow.title: Observe order and count through the API
flow.html:
Tests need not read private links to reveal many representation mistakes. A short operation sequence can check the public consequences: FIFO order and the remaining count. Use different values so a swapped order is visible. Reusing the same value for both additions would conceal that particular error.

queue.add(4);
queue.add(9);
assertEquals(4, queue.remove());
assertEquals(1, queue.size());

flow.title: Try the queue again after it becomes empty
flow.html:
An emptied object must often remain usable. A stale link may not affect the first removal but can break the next addition. The sequence empty → one → empty → one tests that transition. It complements a many-element test because it repeatedly crosses the representation’s empty boundary.

queue.add(4);
assertEquals(4, queue.remove());
queue.add(9);
assertEquals(9, queue.remove());

flow.title: Recognize a chosen sparse-storage rule
flow.html:
Another representation can choose different invariants. Consider a count store indexed by integer keys: reading an absent key returns zero, and setting a count to zero removes its entry. It stores only positive counts. That is this design’s sparse-storage rule, not a Java rule. A stored zero can violate the representation even though a public read still returns zero.

For this design, “no entry for key 7” represents count zero at key 7.

flow.title: Check the promised key order separately
flow.html:
The same count store may require entries in strictly increasing key order. This is a separate invariant from positive stored counts: every count can be valid while the key order is wrong. Check the field named by the rule. Sorting by count instead of key would satisfy a different requirement and can still break lookup assumptions.

Keys 3 then 9 satisfy increasing key order, regardless of whether their counts are 8 and 2.

flow.title: Recognize an array alias
flow.html:
The next representation issue is shared storage. Assigning an array reference to another variable does not copy its elements into a new array. Both variables name the same object: they are aliases. A change made through either reference is visible through the other. This can accidentally change supposedly saved expectations.

int[] original = new int[]{4, 9};
int[] other = original;
other[0] = 7;

flow.title: Copy a primitive array’s contents
flow.html:
Calling clone() on an int array creates another int array with the same element values. The new array has its own element storage. Changing one int element of the copy does not change the original. This differs from simply assigning the original reference to a new variable.

int[] copy = original.clone();
copy[0] = 7; // original[0] stays unchanged

flow.title: Test a snapshot’s independence by mutation
flow.html:
Suppose IntQueue offers int[] toArray(), promising a snapshot whose mutation cannot affect the queue. Equal contents alone do not check that independence. Change the returned array, then inspect the queue through its own API. The expected queue value comes from the original addition, not from the modified snapshot.

int[] snapshot = queue.toArray();
snapshot[0] = 99;
assertEquals(4, queue.remove());

flow.title: Read an array of object references
flow.html:
Arrays can also store references to objects. In Counter[], each element is a Counter reference rather than an int. Storing a Counter in an array does not construct another Counter. Calling a method through counters[0] acts on the same object that was placed in that element.

Counter first = new Counter();
first.set(4);
Counter[] counters = new Counter[]{first};

flow.title: Distinguish shallow copying from deep independence
flow.html:
Cloning an object array copies the array’s references, not the referenced objects. The outer arrays are different, but their corresponding elements can still name the same mutable Counter. This is a shallow copy. It is a defect only when the contract promises deeper independence than that shared storage provides.

Counter[] copy = original.clone();
copy[0].set(9); // the referenced Counter is shared

practice.title: Begin with the queue’s public rule
practice.prompt:
new IntQueue() creates an empty FIFO queue. void add(int value) appends at the back; int remove() removes and returns the oldest value, throwing NoSuchElementException if empty. int size() counts stored values; boolean isEmpty() says whether that count is zero.

After the following setup, what must the first queue.remove() return?

IntQueue queue = new IntQueue();
queue.add(4);
queue.add(9);
practice.hint: FIFO means first in, first out.
practice.solution: It must return 4, the oldest stored value. The queue will then contain only 9.

options.feedback: 4 was added before 9.
Returning the newest value would describe stack-like order, not this queue.
2 is the size before removal, not the oldest value.

practice.title: Name the representation’s links
practice.prompt: In a linked queue, each node has an int value and a Node next reference. head is the first node; tail is the last. There are exactly two nodes: first holds 4 and second holds 9. first.next is second and second.next is null. Which head/tail assignment represents FIFO order 4 then 9?
practice.hint: The first removal uses head; the final node is tail.
practice.solution: head = first and tail = second make the first stored value 4 and the last 9.

options.feedback: These references name the first and last nodes in the chain.
The endpoints are reversed relative to the next links and FIFO order.
A nonempty queue needs a head through which its first node can be reached.

practice.title: Count reachable nodes
practice.prompt: A linked queue’s invariant requires size to equal the number of reachable nodes. Starting at head visits a node holding 4, then a node holding 9, then null. The stored size is 1. Explain the mismatch and the required size. Do not assume which method caused it.
practice.hint: Count the nodes described; distinguish the invalid state from an unproven cause.
practice.solution: Two nodes are reachable, so the invariant requires size 2. The stored value 1 disagrees with the structure. This state is evidence of an inconsistency, but it does not by itself identify the operation that caused it.
rubric: Counts two reachable nodes.
States that size must be 2 rather than 1.
Does not invent an unobserved cause such as a particular missing increment.

practice.title: Represent the empty state consistently
practice.prompt: This queue’s representation requires an empty queue to have size 0, head null, and tail null. After removing its only element, which observed state violates that empty-state rule?
practice.hint: A reference to the removed node is still a non-null reference.
practice.solution: Size 0 and head null do not make a stale non-null tail valid. The tail must also be cleared.

options.text: size is 0; head is null; tail is null.
options.feedback: All three required empty-state facts hold.

options.text: size is 0; head is null; tail still refers to the removed node.
options.feedback: The stale tail violates the required empty representation.

options.text: Before removal: size is 1; head and tail refer to the same final node.
options.feedback: That can be a correct singleton representation before removal.

practice.title: Repair the last-removal transition
practice.prompt:
A linked queue uses Node head, Node tail, and int size. Empty means head and tail are both null and size is 0. A nonempty remove has just executed the two lines below. Write the missing if statement that clears tail only when the removal made the queue empty.

head = head.next;
size--;
// restore the empty-state endpoint rule if needed
practice.hint: Inspect the new head, after advancing it.
practice.solution:
if (head == null) {
    tail = null;
}
rubric: Checks head == null after the head update.
Sets tail = null inside that condition.
Does not clear tail unconditionally when other nodes remain.

practice.title: Observe order and count through the API
practice.prompt:
new IntQueue() creates an empty FIFO queue. void add(int value) appends at the back; int remove() removes and returns the oldest value, throwing NoSuchElementException if empty. int size() counts stored values; boolean isEmpty() says whether that count is zero.

Assume the Jupiter @Test and assertion imports are present. Write the method inside an ordinary test class.

Write void removesInInsertionOrder(). Add 4 then 9; verify both removal values in order, then verify size 0 and isEmpty true.
practice.hint: The expected removal sequence is 4, 9. Use assertEquals for ints and assertTrue for the boolean.
practice.solution:
@Test
void removesInInsertionOrder() {
    IntQueue queue = new IntQueue();
    queue.add(4);
    queue.add(9);
    assertEquals(4, queue.remove());
    assertEquals(9, queue.remove());
    assertEquals(0, queue.size());
    assertTrue(queue.isEmpty());
}
rubric: Creates a fresh queue and adds distinct values 4 then 9.
Checks removal results in FIFO order.
Checks both the final count and the Boolean empty observation.
Uses a valid @Test void method.

practice.title: Try the queue again after it becomes empty
practice.prompt:
new IntQueue() creates an empty FIFO queue. void add(int value) appends at the back; int remove() removes and returns the oldest value, throwing NoSuchElementException if empty. int size() counts stored values; boolean isEmpty() says whether that count is zero.

Which sequence best targets a stale-tail defect left behind when removing the only element?
practice.hint: Reach the empty state by removal, then reuse the same queue.
practice.solution: Add one value, remove it, then add and remove another value on the same object. This exercises the state transition that may depend on a correctly reset tail.

options.text: Create a fresh queue and check size once.
options.feedback: That checks construction, not cleanup after removal.

options.text: Add 4; remove 4; add 9; remove 9 on the same queue.
options.feedback: This crosses through the emptied state and immediately reuses it.

options.text: Create two queues and add one value to each.
options.feedback: Neither object reaches the state after its last removal.

practice.title: Recognize a chosen sparse-storage rule
practice.prompt: A count store’s chosen invariant says stored counts are positive; zero is represented by the absence of an entry. Reading an absent key returns 0. Which internal state violates that invariant?
practice.hint: The design forbids an explicitly stored zero even if its read result seems plausible.
practice.solution: An entry for key 7 with stored count 0 violates the chosen invariant. Removing that entry represents zero correctly.

options.text: Key 7 has no entry; reading it returns 0.
options.feedback: That is the specified representation of a zero count.

options.text: Key 7 has an entry whose stored count is 0.
options.feedback: The representation requires every stored count to be positive.

options.text: Key 7 has an entry whose stored count is 3.
options.feedback: A positive count is allowed to have a stored entry.

practice.title: Check the promised key order separately
practice.prompt: A count store requires positive counts and entries in strictly increasing key order. Its two entries are currently key 9, count 2, followed by key 3, count 8. State the corrected entry order and explain which invariant is broken. Preserve each key’s count.
practice.hint: Order the keys, not the counts, and keep each key/count association together.
practice.solution: The order must be key 3 with count 8, followed by key 9 with count 2. Both counts are already positive; the broken invariant is increasing key order. Swapping counts between keys would change the represented data rather than repair ordering.
rubric: Places key 3 before key 9.
Keeps count 8 with key 3 and count 2 with key 9.
Identifies ordering as the broken invariant and does not confuse it with positive-count validity.

practice.title: Recognize an array alias
practice.prompt:
After these statements, what is original[0]?

int[] original = new int[]{4, 9};
int[] other = original;
other[0] = 7;
practice.hint: original and other refer to one array object.
practice.solution: original[0] is 7 because the assignment created a second reference to the same array.

options.feedback: That would require independent array storage, which assignment did not create.
The mutation is visible through both aliases.

options.text: It is a compile error because arrays cannot be assigned.
options.feedback: Compatible array reference assignment is legal; it does not copy contents.

practice.title: Copy a primitive array’s contents
practice.prompt: int[] original = new int[]{4, 9}; already exists. Write one declaration that creates an independent int-array copy using clone and stores it in copy.
practice.hint: Call clone on original; declare the result as int[].
practice.solution: int[] copy = original.clone();
rubric: Declares int[] copy.
Calls original.clone(), not just original.
Uses a complete assignment statement with a semicolon.

practice.title: Test a snapshot’s independence by mutation
practice.prompt:
new IntQueue() creates an empty FIFO queue. void add(int value) appends at the back; int remove() removes and returns the oldest value, throwing NoSuchElementException if empty. int size() counts stored values; boolean isEmpty() says whether that count is zero.

int[] toArray() returns queue values from oldest to newest in an independent snapshot. Write the statements after the supplied setup to mutate the first snapshot element to 99 and verify that the queue still removes 4. Assertion imports are present.

IntQueue queue = new IntQueue();
queue.add(4);
int[] snapshot = queue.toArray();
practice.hint: Mutate snapshot, then observe queue; do not use the changed snapshot as your expected value.
practice.solution:
snapshot[0] = 99;
assertEquals(4, queue.remove());
rubric: Changes snapshot[0] to 99.
Observes the queue with remove().
Uses the independent expected value 4.

practice.title: Read an array of object references
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

What does first.get() return after these statements?

Counter first = new Counter();
first.set(4);
Counter[] counters = new Counter[]{first};
counters[0].set(9);
practice.hint: The array element and first name the same Counter object.
practice.solution: It returns 9. The array stores a reference to first; it did not create a separate Counter.

options.feedback: The existing Counter was mutated through the array reference.
Both references lead to the same Counter.
No second default-valued Counter was constructed.

practice.title: Distinguish shallow copying from deep independence
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

The following code produces two arrays. Explain the value of original[0].get() afterward, and why different array identities do not prove independent Counter objects.

Counter first = new Counter();
first.set(4);
Counter[] original = new Counter[]{first};
Counter[] copy = original.clone();
copy[0].set(9);
practice.hint: clone copies the Counter reference stored in element zero.
practice.solution: original[0].get() is 9. The clone creates a different outer array, but both element-zero references still name first. Deep independence would require separate mutable Counter objects as well; whether that is required depends on the copy contract.
rubric: Predicts the observed value 9.
Distinguishes new outer-array identity from shared element identity.
Explains that the mutable Counter object is shared.
Makes independence a contract question rather than declaring every shallow copy wrong.

bridge: You can now detect a bad internal state or an unexpected shared object. Next, inspect tests themselves for the same kinds of false assumptions.

title: Find the defect in the test itself
summary: Check argument types, expectations, assertion meaning, fixtures, and exception scope before trusting a green or red result.
goals: Separate a test compilation error from a wrong expectation or weak assertion.
Keep expectations and fixtures independent of the behavior under test.
Repair an exception test so only its named action can satisfy it.
setup: Return to Counter and reuse the syntax already learned. The production contract is fixed while we inspect one defective test at a time.

flow.title: Check the argument’s type first
flow.html:
Before judging an expected value, make sure the test can call the method. Counter.set requires an int. Quotes create a String, even when the text looks numeric. A test with the wrong argument type cannot run, so it cannot yet provide evidence that the production method accepts or rejects a value.

counter.set("4"); // String supplied where int is required

flow.title: Derive the expectation from the rule
flow.html:
A test can compile while asking for the wrong behavior. Counter.set replaces the old value; it does not add to it. If the old value is 4 and we set 5, the expected result is 5. Read that rule independently before inspecting what the current implementation happens to return.

counter.set(4);
counter.set(5);
assertEquals(5, counter.get());

flow.title: Put expected before actual
flow.html:
For a simple value comparison, reversing the two arguments can still detect a mismatch. However, it labels the diagnostic incorrectly: JUnit reports the first argument as expected. Keep the contract-derived value first and the observed value second so a failure report can be read without mentally reversing its meaning.

assertEquals(5, counter.get());

flow.title: Match the assertion to the expression type
flow.html:
assertTrue needs a boolean condition. Counter.get returns an int, so passing get directly to assertTrue is a type error. To compare its exact numeric result, use assertEquals. Alternatively, an explicit comparison such as counter.get() == 5 is boolean, although assertEquals gives clearer value diagnostics.

assertEquals(5, counter.get());

flow.title: Notice when nothing checks the result
flow.html:
An @Test annotation makes a method runnable by JUnit; it does not create an expectation. Printing a value or assigning it to a local variable is observation without an assertion. Such a test can still fail on an unexpected exception, but a wrong ordinary return value will pass unnoticed.

counter.set(5);
int actual = counter.get();
// actual is never compared with 5

flow.title: Reject a self-comparison as an oracle
flow.html:
A test needs an expectation independent of the result it is checking. Comparing a stored actual value with itself is guaranteed to match for this int, even if the production result is wrong. A passing assertion can therefore still be useless. Replace the self-comparison with a contract-derived expectation.

int actual = counter.get();
assertEquals(actual, actual); // no independent expectation

flow.title: Start each stateful test from its own fixture
flow.html:
A test should not need another test to run first. In ordinary Jupiter tests, a new test-class instance is normally created for each test method, so one method’s instance-field changes do not prepare another. Static shared fields introduce different risks. Arrange the required Counter state inside the test or in a per-test setup method.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(4); // this test establishes its own starting state

flow.title: Locate the source of the expected exception
flow.html:
An exception assertion accepts a matching exception from anywhere inside its lambda. If preparation inside the lambda throws first, the named target call may never run. Keep valid setup outside the checked action. Then a matching exception is evidence about the intended call rather than an earlier statement.

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> {
    counter.set(-2);
    counter.set(-1);
});

flow.title: Repair the scope of the exception check
flow.html:
Repairing the previous test means controlling both its starting state and its checked action. First establish a valid value, outside the lambda. Then place only the negative target call in assertThrows. The unchanged-state assertion belongs afterward. These locations make each line’s role visible and avoid a misleading success from setup.

counter.set(4);
assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
    () -> counter.set(-1));
assertEquals(4, counter.get());

flow.title: Keep expected storage independent too
flow.html:
Independence also applies to mutable expected objects. If expected and input name the same array, a production method can mutate both names at once. The assertion may then compare two views of the same wrong contents. Build expected separately when the requirement says the input must be preserved.

int[] input = new int[]{4, 9};
int[] expected = new int[]{4, 9};

flow.title: Repair a small test as a whole
flow.html:
Finish the audit in a useful order: does it compile, does it call the intended operation, and does its assertion express the contract? These are separate questions. Repairing syntax alone is not enough if the expected value still describes the wrong behavior. Reuse a fresh fixture and the smallest meaningful comparison.

For Counter.set, the intended observation is the replacement value returned by get.

practice.title: Check the argument’s type first
practice.prompt:
Counter declares only void set(int next). A valid variable Counter counter exists. Classify this test statement:

counter.set("4");
practice.hint: The quotation marks determine the expression’s type.
practice.solution: This is a compile-time argument-type error. The required int call is counter.set(4).

options.text: It runs and checks whether numeric text is parsed.
options.feedback: The API has no String overload or parsing contract.

options.text: It fails to compile because "4" is a String.
options.feedback: A String argument cannot be passed to the stated int parameter.
The source does not compile, so no runtime exception is reached.

practice.title: Derive the expectation from the rule
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

What is wrong with this test’s final expectation?

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(4);
counter.set(5);
assertEquals(9, counter.get());
practice.hint: The operation is set, not add.
practice.solution: The expected value must be 5. Expecting 9 incorrectly specifies addition, so a correct set implementation would fail this test.

options.text: The test expects addition although set promises replacement.
options.feedback: The oracle is wrong even though the types and assertion syntax are valid.
JUnit can compare int values.

options.text: The second call must be inside assertThrows.
options.feedback: The nonnegative value 5 is valid and should be accepted.

practice.title: Put expected before actual
practice.prompt:
A Counter should contain 5 after counter.set(5). Repair the assertion’s argument order so its diagnostic labels expected and actual correctly. Assume assertion imports.

assertEquals(counter.get(), 5);
practice.hint: Expected 5 belongs first.
practice.solution:
assertEquals(5, counter.get());

The original can compile, but it reverses the expected/actual labels.
rubric: Places literal 5 first.
Places counter.get() second.
Does not claim the original is necessarily a compile error.

practice.title: Match the assertion to the expression type
practice.prompt: An existing, non-null Counter counter is available. int Counter.get() should return 5 here. Which assertion directly checks that exact value and compiles with Jupiter?
practice.hint: An int value is not itself a boolean.
practice.solution: assertEquals(5, counter.get()) compares the expected int with the actual int.

options.feedback: get returns int, which cannot serve as assertTrue’s Boolean condition.
The value assertion fits the method’s return type and the requirement.
The literal 5 is also an int, not a boolean condition.

practice.title: Notice when nothing checks the result
practice.prompt:
The contract says set(5) must store 5. Explain what this test fails to check, then write one assertion that closes the gap. get() returns int; imports are present.

@Test
void storesFive() {
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    counter.set(5);
    int actual = counter.get();
}
practice.hint: The variable records a value but does not decide whether it is correct.
practice.solution:
The test never compares the observed value with the contractual result, so an ordinary wrong value can pass. Add:

assertEquals(5, actual);
rubric: Identifies that no assertion checks actual.
Does not claim the test can never fail for any reason.
Adds assertEquals with expected 5 and actual as the observed value.

practice.title: Reject a self-comparison as an oracle
practice.prompt:
After counter.set(5), get must return 5. A faulty implementation returns 9. What happens to this assertion?

int actual = counter.get();
assertEquals(actual, actual);
practice.hint: Both arguments are the same stored int value.
practice.solution: It compares 9 with 9 and passes. The required assertion is assertEquals(5, actual).

options.text: It fails because JUnit knows set should store 5.
options.feedback: JUnit knows only the expectation supplied in the test, not the domain contract.

options.text: It passes because both arguments contain 9.
options.feedback: The assertion compares the result with itself.

options.text: It cannot compile because both arguments use the same variable.
options.feedback: Self-comparison is legal; it is weak test design here.

practice.title: Start each stateful test from its own fixture
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

A test named storesFive assumes a different test already created and prepared its Counter. Explain why that dependency is unreliable, then give the two setup statements for an independent Counter initially containing 4.
practice.hint: Each test must establish its own prerequisites, regardless of execution order or test-instance lifecycle.
practice.solution:
Tests may run independently, and Jupiter’s ordinary per-method instances do not share instance-field mutations. The test should arrange its own state:

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(4);
rubric: Explains the unsafe dependence on another test’s execution or state.
Creates a new Counter in the local test setup.
Calls set(4) before the behavior being tested.

practice.title: Locate the source of the expected exception
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

The test claims to verify rejection of -1, and counter is a valid object. With a correct Counter, which call supplies the exception that makes this assertion pass?

    counter.set(-2);
    counter.set(-1);
});
practice.hint: Execution stops at the first thrown exception.
practice.solution: set(-2) throws first. The target set(-1) never executes, so this green assertion does not check its named case.

options.text: set(-1), because it is the last statement.
options.feedback: The earlier exception prevents execution from reaching the last statement.

options.text: set(-2), before the target call can execute.
options.feedback: Any matching exception in the lambda can satisfy assertThrows.

options.text: Both calls must throw before assertThrows passes.
options.feedback: A single thrown exception exits the lambda; the rest is skipped.

practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

Assume the Jupiter @Test and assertion imports are present. Write the method inside an ordinary test class.

rubric: Uses a fresh Counter and valid setup outside assertThrows.
Checks IllegalArgumentException.class.
Contains only counter.set(-1) in the lambda.

practice.title: Keep expected storage independent too
practice.prompt:
static int ArrayStats.sum(int[] values) must return the sum without changing its non-null input. The test below tries to check input preservation. Explain its weakness, then replace only the expected-array declaration with an independent one.

int[] expected = input;

assertArrayEquals(expected, input);
