practice.solution:
Expected aliases input, so both names see any accidental mutation. Preserve an independent contractual snapshot:

int[] expected = new int[]{4, 9};
rubric: Identifies that expected and input refer to the same array.
Explains how shared mutation can produce a false pass.
Creates a separate array containing 4 and 9.

practice.title: Repair a small test as a whole
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

Assume the Jupiter @Test and assertion imports are present. Write the method inside an ordinary test class.

Repair this complete method so it verifies that setting 5 after 4 replaces the value. Explain the two original problems briefly after your corrected method.

@Test
void replacesValue() {
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    counter.set(4);
    counter.set("5");
    assertEquals(9, counter.get());
}
practice.hint: There is one argument-type error and one wrong expected value.
practice.solution:
@Test
void replacesValue() {
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    counter.set(4);
    counter.set(5);
    assertEquals(5, counter.get());
}

Quoted "5" is a String, incompatible with the int parameter. Expected 9 incorrectly treats set as addition; the replacement contract requires 5.
rubric: Replaces the String argument with int 5.
Uses contractual expected value 5 rather than 9.
Keeps the setup and state observation in a complete valid test method.
Explains the compile-time type problem separately from the incorrect oracle.

bridge: A trustworthy test gives you useful evidence. Next, record that evidence so another person can reproduce and diagnose the failure.

title: Record an error so someone can reproduce it
summary: Build a precise defect record, read its evidence, and attach an exception correctly to a Java log record.
goals: Write reproducible steps with separate expected and observed outcomes.
Distinguish a failure location, an observation, and a supported cause.
Use Logger.log with a level, context message, and the original exception object.
setup: Use a Counter replacement defect for the report. Then learn the small Java logging API needed to retain a caught exception’s diagnostic details.

flow.title: Make the starting state reproducible
flow.html:
A defect record needs enough setup to reproduce the observation. “Setting five gives eight” omits the earlier value. For this Counter, the revealing sequence starts fresh, stores 3, and then stores 5. Record that order exactly. A call on a fresh zero-valued object may hide a defect that accidentally adds instead of replacing.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(3);
counter.set(5);
int actual = counter.get();

flow.title: Separate expected from observed
flow.html:
The expected result is what the contract requires; the observed result is what this run produced. Keep them in separate fields even when the difference looks obvious. Here, replacing 3 with 5 requires 5, whereas the observed 8 is evidence of failure. Do not copy the observed result into the expected field.

Expected: get returns 5. Observed: get returns 8.

flow.title: Read a stack frame as a location
flow.html:
A stack trace records the calls associated with a failure. A frame such as CounterTest.replacesValue(CounterTest.java:18) identifies a method, file, and line. For an assertion failure, that line may be where the mismatch was detected. It does not automatically identify the production statement that caused the wrong value.

CounterTest.replacesValue(CounterTest.java:18) points to the test’s detection site.

flow.title: Support the cause with code evidence
flow.html:
The observed value is a symptom. A cause explains how the code produced it. If inspection shows value += next, you can connect the old 3 and new 5 to the observed 8. Without that inspection, addition would be a hypothesis. Mark the difference between what you observed and what you have verified.

value += next; // adds instead of replacing

flow.title: Connect several symptoms to one invariant
flow.html:
A report should not assume that every symptom has a separate cause. Recall the queue invariant: size equals reachable nodes. If removing the last node forgets to decrease size, size can be wrong and isEmpty can also be wrong when it uses that field. One missing update can therefore explain several observations; record that causal link.

boolean isEmpty() {
    return size == 0;
}

flow.title: Record the version that was actually run
flow.html:
Code and tests change, so a reproducible record identifies the version tested. Include useful environment details when they affect interpretation: the code revision, Java version, JUnit version, and the test name. Record known facts rather than guessed versions. A title should describe the behavior clearly enough to recognize the issue later.

Title: Setting a new Counter value adds to the previous value.

flow.title: Assemble a compact defect record
flow.html:
Combine the fields you have practiced: a clear title, exact steps, expected result, observed result, and evidence. A proposed correction is not a verified fix. Label the current status accurately until the repaired code has been run against the reproducing test. Keep the report factual enough for someone else to confirm it.

A short record with exact evidence is more useful than a long description without a reproducible case.

flow.title: Introduce a logger as a separate tool
flow.html:
A defect report describes a case for a reader. A logger records events while an application runs. Java supplies java.util.logging.Logger; importing it makes the short name Logger available in the source file. It is a production diagnostic tool, not a replacement for assertions that decide whether a test passes.

import java.util.logging.Logger;

flow.title: Obtain a named logger
flow.html:
Logger.getLogger(name) obtains a logger with that name. It is a static call, like other class-level factory methods you have used. Store the returned Logger in a variable before calling its instance methods. The name identifies a logging category; it does not by itself choose a file or guarantee that a record will be displayed.

Logger logger = Logger.getLogger("training.counter");

flow.title: Choose the supplied severity level
flow.html:
A log call also carries a level describing the event’s severity. Level.WARNING is a named value supplied by java.util.logging.Level. A project decides which situations deserve each level. We will use WARNING for this example’s rejected update; the level is not a Java exception type and is not a JUnit outcome.

import java.util.logging.Level;
// Level.WARNING is the level chosen for this example.

flow.title: Attach the original exception
flow.html:
The overload log(Level, String, Throwable) takes a level, a context message, and an exception object. Passing the original exception attaches its stack and cause information to the record. Handlers and formatters decide how records are emitted. Passing only the exception’s message would supply text rather than the original diagnostic object.

logger.log(Level.WARNING, "Counter update failed", ex);

flow.title: Keep cause information available
flow.html:
An exception’s message is only one part of its evidence. A wrapper may retain an earlier exception as its cause, and each layer can have a stack trace. Logging ex makes that exception object available to the logging system. Logging ex.getMessage() alone does not retain the object or its cause chain.

logger.log(Level.WARNING, "Update failed", ex);

flow.title: Do not confuse recording with handling
flow.html:
A log call records an event; it does not automatically rethrow an exception or fail a test. The surrounding method’s contract still determines what happens next. If this wrapper promises to record the failure and propagate the original exception, it must do both explicitly. A silent normal return would change the caller-visible behavior.

logger.log(Level.WARNING, "Counter update failed", ex);
throw ex;

practice.title: Make the starting state reproducible
practice.prompt:
Observed case: new Counter() starts at 0; set(int next) is documented to replace the stored value. Calling set(3), then set(5), makes get() return 8 in the version being investigated.

Which reproduction includes the state needed for the observed failure?
practice.hint: The previous stored value affects this particular defect.
practice.solution: Create a new Counter, call set(3), then set(5), then observe get. That recreates the exact operation sequence.

options.feedback: This omits the starting state and may produce a different result.

options.text: Create a Counter; set 3; set 5; read get.
options.feedback: This specifies the complete observed sequence.

options.text: Restart the computer and try again.
options.feedback: This does not identify the relevant input or object state.

practice.title: Separate expected from observed
practice.prompt:
Observed case: new Counter() starts at 0; set(int next) is documented to replace the stored value. Calling set(3), then set(5), makes get() return 8 in the version being investigated.

Write two short report lines, one labelled Expected and one labelled Observed. Base the expected result on the replacement contract.
practice.hint: A setter replaces the prior value; it does not add to it.
practice.solution:
Expected: after set(3), then set(5), get returns 5.
Observed: get returns 8 in the investigated version.
rubric: Labels the expected outcome as 5.
Labels the observed outcome as 8.
Connects both outcomes to the stated operation sequence.

practice.title: Read a stack frame as a location
practice.prompt: An assertion failure says expected 5 but was 8. Its first user-code frame is CounterTest.replacesValue(CounterTest.java:18), and line 18 contains assertEquals(5, counter.get());. What does that frame establish?
practice.hint: A detection site and a root cause need not be the same line.
practice.solution: It establishes where the test detected the mismatch. Inspect the production execution separately before assigning a root cause.

options.text: Line 18 detected the mismatch in the test.
options.feedback: The frame identifies the failing assertion’s location.

options.text: Line 18 proves assertEquals itself is defective.
options.feedback: A correct assertion can report a defect in the value supplied to it.

options.text: The first stack frame always identifies the production root cause.
options.feedback: A stack trace is execution evidence, not an automatic causal diagnosis.

practice.title: Support the cause with code evidence
practice.prompt:
Observed case: new Counter() starts at 0; set(int next) is documented to replace the stored value. Calling set(3), then set(5), makes get() return 8 in the version being investigated.

Inspection confirms that set(int next) ends with value += next;. Explain why this line accounts for the observed 8, and name the replacement statement required by the contract.
practice.hint: Expand += into value = value + next.
practice.solution: value += next computes the old 3 plus the new 5, giving 8. The replacement contract requires value = next;. The statement links the observed symptom to a supported cause.
rubric: Explains 3 + 5 = 8 using the confirmed += statement.
Distinguishes the symptom from the causal statement.
Identifies value = next; as the required replacement operation.

practice.title: Connect several symptoms to one invariant
practice.prompt: A linked queue requires size to equal reachable nodes. After its only node is removed, head and tail are null, but size remains 1 and isEmpty(), implemented as return size == 0;, returns false. Inspection confirms remove advanced the links but omitted size--;. Explain the shared cause of both public symptoms.
practice.hint: Both size() and isEmpty() depend on the same stale size field.
practice.solution: No nodes remain, so the correct size is 0 and isEmpty should be true. The missing decrement leaves size at 1; size() reports that wrong field and isEmpty computes false from it. Both symptoms follow from one broken size-versus-reachable-nodes invariant, so the evidence supports one shared cause.
rubric: Connects zero reachable nodes to required size 0.
Explains the observed size 1 using the confirmed missing decrement.
Explains false isEmpty as a consequence of that same stale field.
Does not assume two independent defects are required.

practice.title: Record the version that was actually run
practice.prompt: You are writing a reproducible test-failure record. Select the useful facts to include when known.
practice.hint: Prefer details that let another person locate the code and repeat the same case.
practice.solution: The revision and runtime/test versions identify the run; the test name and exact steps locate and reproduce the failure.

options.text: The code revision and Java/JUnit versions actually used.
options.feedback: These identify which implementation and tools produced the result.

options.text: A guessed version number so no field is blank.
options.feedback: Invented metadata makes reproduction less reliable; mark unknown facts honestly.

options.text: The test name and precise input/setup sequence.
options.feedback: These help someone locate and repeat the failing case.

options.text: Only “does not work,” without inputs or outcomes.
options.feedback: That gives no reproducible or checkable description.

practice.title: Assemble a compact defect record
practice.prompt:
Observed case: new Counter() starts at 0; set(int next) is documented to replace the stored value. Calling set(3), then set(5), makes get() return 8 in the version being investigated.

Given facts: test CounterTest.replacesValue; revision counter-a; Java 11 and Jupiter 5.10.5; inspected setter uses value += next;; no repair has been run. Write a compact report with title, run context, steps, expected, observed, cause, and status.
practice.hint: Do not mark a proposed change as verified.
practice.solution:
Title: Setting a Counter value adds to its previous value
Run: counter-a; Java 11; Jupiter 5.10.5
Test: CounterTest.replacesValue
Steps: create Counter; set(3); set(5); call get()
Expected: 5, because set replaces the value
Observed: 8
Cause: value += next adds 3 and 5 instead of replacing 3
Proposed correction: value = next
Status: reproduced; correction not yet verified
rubric: Gives the exact fresh-object/set(3)/set(5)/get sequence.
Separates expected 5 from observed 8.
Includes the supplied run context and test name accurately.
Connects the inspected += statement to the symptom.
States that the proposed correction has not been verified.

practice.title: Introduce a logger as a separate tool
practice.prompt: A Java source file will declare a variable with type Logger from the standard java.util.logging package. Which import makes that simple type name available?
practice.hint: Import the fully qualified class name followed by a semicolon.
practice.solution: import java.util.logging.Logger;

options.feedback: This imports the standard Logger class.
Logger is not the JUnit annotation or assertion API.
An annotation does not import this class.

practice.title: Obtain a named logger
practice.prompt: java.util.logging.Logger is imported. Write one declaration that obtains the logger named "training.counter" and stores it in a variable named logger.
practice.hint: The type and factory class are both Logger; the local variable is lowercase logger.
practice.solution: Logger logger = Logger.getLogger("training.counter");
rubric: Declares a Logger variable named logger.
Calls the static method Logger.getLogger.
Passes the stated String name and ends with a semicolon.

practice.title: Choose the supplied severity level
practice.prompt: The application’s logging rule says a rejected Counter update is recorded at WARNING. java.util.logging.Level is imported. Which expression supplies that level to a Logger call?
practice.hint: Use the named value on Level, not a String or exception class.
practice.solution: Level.WARNING is the logging-level object used as the first argument.

options.feedback: This is a String, not the Level value required by the described overload.
This selects the named WARNING level.
This is a class literal for an exception type, not a logging severity.

practice.title: Attach the original exception
practice.prompt: Logger logger already exists; Level is imported. Inside catch (IllegalArgumentException ex), write one log call at Level.WARNING with context "Counter update failed", attaching the caught exception itself.
practice.hint: The third argument is ex, not ex.getMessage().
practice.solution: logger.log(Level.WARNING, "Counter update failed", ex);
rubric: Calls logger.log with Level.WARNING first.
Uses the stated context String second.
Passes the original ex as the third argument.

practice.title: Keep cause information available
practice.prompt: ex is an IllegalStateException whose cause is the original update failure. logger and Level are available. Which call attaches the complete exception object to the record?
practice.hint: Look for ex as the Throwable argument.
practice.solution: The three-argument call passes the original exception object. Its message, stack, and linked cause remain available, although output depends on the configured logging handlers.

options.feedback: This records message text only; it does not attach the exception object.
The third argument is the Throwable object whose details and cause can be inspected.
This generic text includes neither the original exception object nor its diagnostic details.

practice.title: Do not confuse recording with handling
practice.prompt:
A wrapper promises to log and propagate the original IllegalArgumentException. logger exists and Level is imported. Complete this catch body with the missing statement after the log call.

    logger.log(Level.WARNING, "Counter update failed", ex);
    // propagate the same exception
}
practice.hint: Logging does not replace the ordinary throw statement.
practice.solution:
throw ex;

This retains the promised propagation. In a test, a logging statement alone would also not establish pass or fail.
rubric: Uses throw ex; to propagate the same object.
Keeps the log call and propagation as separate actions.
Does not replace the exception with a new message-only object.

bridge: You have a reproducible failure and a clear record of it. Next, use that evidence to validate a repair and retain a regression test.

title: Keep a failing case as a regression test
summary: Repair a boundary defect, preserve its witness, and distinguish a code fix from an explicitly changed contract.
goals: Keep an independent expected result while making the production fix.
Select neighboring cases and state checks that challenge the repair.
Update tests for an explicit contract revision without weakening them to match a defect.
setup: Return to Counter.set and focus on one faulty boundary: rejecting zero even though the contract accepts it.

flow.title: Keep the contractual expectation
flow.html:
A regression test preserves a case that once exposed a defect. Suppose Counter wrongly rejects zero. The correct expectation remains that zero is accepted; changing the test to expect rejection would preserve the defect instead. Begin with a failing test whose result follows the documented contract.

counter.set(0);
assertEquals(0, counter.get());

flow.title: Trace the boundary condition
flow.html:
Read the failing input against the guard. With next equal to zero, next <= 0 is true, so execution throws before the assignment. The contract rejects only values below zero. This local trace identifies the extra equality case admitted by the rejection condition.

if (next <= 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");
}
value = next;

flow.title: Make the smallest contract-preserving repair
flow.html:
A focused repair changes the faulty condition while retaining required rejection. Deleting the guard would accept zero but also accept negatives. Changing <= to < corrects this boundary without abandoning the rest of the contract. Keep the assignment after the guard so invalid inputs cannot mutate the field.

if (next < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");
}
value = next;

flow.title: Challenge the neighboring cases
flow.html:
After the revealing zero case passes, test the nearest values on each side. Minus one should still be rejected; one should still be stored. This small group checks whether the repair shifted the boundary correctly. It does not prove every aspect of the method, but it targets the concrete risk created by changing the guard.

-1 → reject, 0 → store 0, 1 → store 1.

flow.title: Keep the exact revealing test
flow.html:
A useful regression test remains small and recognizable. Establish a nonzero value, then set zero and verify zero was stored. Starting at a nonzero value also catches an implementation that merely ignores the zero request. A test that begins and ends at zero could miss that no-op defect.

counter.set(4);
counter.set(0);
assertEquals(0, counter.get());

flow.title: Do not weaken the observation
flow.html:
A green result is useful only if the assertion still checks the promised behavior. Replacing an exact-value assertion with a broad property can hide the original defect. Counter storing some nonnegative number does not establish that set stored the requested value. Keep the observation precise enough to distinguish the required result from plausible wrong ones.

assertTrue(counter.get() >= 0); // too weak for “stores 5”

flow.title: Interpret a passing repair honestly
flow.html:
When the original failing test and its focused neighbors pass, you have evidence that those cases work after the change. You do not yet have proof of every method or input. Run the relevant existing tests too, because a change can affect another promised behavior. Expand testing to address a concrete risk, not simply to accumulate green results.

Passing zero, -1, and 1 tests supports the boundary repair for those checked outcomes.

flow.title: Recognize an explicit contract revision
flow.html:
Sometimes requirements intentionally change. That differs from changing a test just to match a defect. If an approved new contract adds an upper limit of 99, an old acceptance test for 100 must be reviewed against the new version. Document the changed rule and its effective version so the revised expectation has an independent basis.

Old rule: every nonnegative int accepted. Revised rule: only 0 through 99 accepted.

flow.title: Retain the unchanged rejection guarantee
flow.html:
Return to the original nonnegative Counter contract. A boundary repair must not break unchanged-state rejection. Write a second focused test from a valid nonzero starting state, then attempt a negative value. Keeping this separate from the zero test gives a useful failure name if a later edit moves validation after mutation.

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
    () -> counter.set(-1));
assertEquals(6, counter.get());

practice.title: Keep the contractual expectation
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

The implementation currently throws for set(0). Which test expectation should be kept while repairing it?
practice.hint: Zero is nonnegative under the given contract.
practice.solution: The test should require normal completion and stored value 0. The current exception is the defect, not a new expected outcome.

options.text: Expect IllegalArgumentException because the current version throws it.
options.feedback: That copies the defective behavior into the oracle.

options.text: Require set(0) to complete and get() to return 0.
options.feedback: This follows the acceptance boundary in the contract.

options.text: Delete every zero test because it fails.
options.feedback: That removes the revealing evidence rather than fixing the cause.

practice.title: Trace the boundary condition
practice.prompt:
set(int next) must accept nonnegative ints and reject negatives. Explain why this body rejects a valid input when next is 0. Name the exact condition that needs changing.

if (next <= 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must be nonnegative");

flow.title: Read only the API types first
flow.html:
We will test a small name validator without seeing its implementation. Start with its header: static boolean isValid(String text). It accepts one String and returns a boolean. The class name is NameRules, so the call is made on that class. Do not decide the expected result until you read the behavior rule.

flow.title: Apply the ordinary valid-case rule
flow.html:
Now read the behavior: valid text has 2–8 characters, all ASCII letters. “Ada” has three characters, and each is in A–Z or a–z, so the expected boolean is true. This reasoning uses the contract alone. You do not need to guess which loop or library method the implementation might use.

flow.title: Choose the lower-boundary pair
flow.html:
The lower accepted length is two. Compare a one-character String with a two-character String while keeping every character valid. That isolates the length boundary. Using a digit or space at the same time would mix two obligations and make a failing result harder to interpret.

"A" → false; "Al" → true.

flow.title: Choose the upper-boundary pair
flow.html:
Apply the same reasoning at the upper edge. Eight letters are accepted; nine letters are rejected. Write the concrete String values rather than merely saying “test the boundary.” Counting these short examples also prevents a test description from claiming one length while its actual input has another.

"Abcdefgh" has 8 characters; "Abcdefghi" has 9.

flow.title: Isolate a disallowed character
flow.html:
Character validation is a separate obligation. Keep length valid and introduce one forbidden character. For example, “A1” has length two but contains a digit, so it must be false. The contract also says no trimming: spaces are actual input characters, not permission to silently change the supplied String.

NameRules.isValid("A1"); // expected false

flow.title: Keep null separate from empty
flow.html:
An empty String is an object with length zero. It therefore follows the ordinary invalid-length rule and returns false. Null is the absence of a String reference and has a separate exception rule here. Treating both as “nothing” would lead to the wrong assertion for one of them.

assertFalse(NameRules.isValid(""));

flow.title: Write the Boolean assertion
flow.html:
For a valid name, the expected result is true, so assertTrue directly checks the method’s boolean. Keep the String argument inside the production call and the production result inside the assertion. The semicolon ends the complete assertion statement. No numeric expected value belongs in this Boolean test.

flow.title: Give the lower-edge case a method
flow.html:

}

flow.title: Write the separate null test
flow.html:
Now use the exception branch of the contract. The delayed action in assertThrows should contain only the validator call with null. The method promises NullPointerException but no exact message, so a message check would add an unsupported requirement. A normal return or an unrelated exception should make this test fail.

assertThrows(NullPointerException.class,
    () -> NameRules.isValid(null));

flow.html:
The test file now needs only the familiar outer pieces: the Test import, assertion imports, and a class containing the method. Keep the class simple. For this independent upper-boundary case, reuse the input you counted earlier and the Boolean assertion you have already practiced. The implementation remains unseen.

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

Without an implementation, you cannot claim a particular branch or statement coverage percentage. A test plan can be well justified while remaining honest about which evidence is unavailable.

Contract evidence chooses inputs and expected outcomes; implementation evidence is needed to measure executed code paths.

static int IntStats.countAtLeast(int[] values, int floor) accepts a non-null array and returns how many elements are greater than or equal to floor. It returns 0 for an empty array and does not change the array.

Test defect: expecting 0 copies that wrong result; the regression test must expect 1. These are proposed corrections until the revised code and tests are run.

bridge: You have combined a contract, a path trace, a repaired test, and a report. The final lesson gives you independent decisions using the same core skills.

title: Choose, write, and explain independently
summary: Practice one decision at a time across copies, state changes, exceptions, and exact object-valued arithmetic.
goals: Select a test from its contract, input type, and observable outcome.
Read weak or defective tests and supply a concrete correction.
Write a complete independent test and describe the limits of its evidence.
setup: Reuse the familiar arrays, Counter, and BigInteger APIs. Each task supplies its own contract so you can reason without hidden context.

flow.title: Choose the source of the test case
flow.html:
Begin with a copying operation on the int arrays you already know. Its contract promises equal contents in a different, independent array. With no implementation supplied, derive cases from those promises: normal contents, empty input, null, and independence. That is black-box design, even though you can imagine how a copy might be implemented.

A guessed implementation is not evidence about actual branches.

flow.title: Choose a content assertion
flow.html:
Array contents and array identity are different observations. To compare element values in order, use assertArrayEquals. A variable holding an expected array does not need to refer to the same object as the result. Keep that expected array independent of the production output so a shared defect cannot change both expectations together.

assertArrayEquals(new int[]{4, 9}, actual);

flow.title: Check the different-array promise
flow.html:
Equal contents can be achieved by returning the input itself, but this copy contract also promises a different array. Use assertNotSame to check that identity relationship. The promise applies to empty arrays too. An empty array is still an object with identity; it is not the same thing as null.

assertNotSame(input, actual);

flow.title: Prove a concrete independence observation
flow.html:
Mutation gives a behavioral check of independence. After copying, change one element of the result and inspect the original. The expected original value comes from the setup. This one observation exposes a returned alias: both variables would then see the changed value. It does not require reading any private implementation.

actual[0] = 99;
assertEquals(4, input[0]);

flow.title: Read the implementation’s alias defect
flow.html:
Now a tiny implementation is visible: it returns values directly. That preserves contents at the instant of return but returns the same reference. The earlier independence test supplies a witness: changing result[0] also changes input[0]. Connect the statement to that observation instead of merely calling the method “not a real copy.”

static int[] copy(int[] values) {
    if (values == null) {
        throw new NullPointerException();
    }
    return values;
}

flow.title: Keep the null action narrow
flow.html:
Return to the exception rule for the same copying API. Null is one reference input; it does not need an array allocation or a failing setup action. Put the single call inside assertThrows. Check the specified type without inventing message text. This gives the assertion one clear source for its expected exception.

assertThrows(NullPointerException.class,
    () -> ArrayCopies.copy(null));

flow.title: Handle a void state change correctly
flow.html:
Switch back to the familiar Counter. Unlike copy, set returns no value: its result is observed through object state. A test cannot place a void call where assertEquals expects an actual value. Perform the action first, then call get. This is the same input → operation → observation pattern with a different return shape.

counter.set(5);
assertEquals(5, counter.get());

flow.title: Audit an old-style exception test
flow.html:
The same rejection can be checked with manual try/catch, but every path must be considered. A catch-only test observes the exceptional path and can leave the normal-return path unchecked. Read the whole test, not just the assertion’s presence. A useful correction identifies where the missing-exception failure belongs.

try {
    counter.set(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
}

flow.title: Match an exact-number object parameter
flow.html:
One final type transfer uses the familiar BigInteger class. A BigInteger parameter requires a compatible object reference, not an int literal or a String. BigInteger.valueOf(4) constructs the required value through a factory method. Decimal text can also be passed to the BigInteger constructor; it is not automatically converted by the production call.

BigNumbers.addOne(BigInteger.valueOf(4));

flow.title: Compare like value types in the oracle
flow.html:
The expected result should also be a BigInteger. Jupiter’s object comparison can compile with mismatched object types, so compilation alone does not guarantee a correct oracle. Comparing integer 5 with BigInteger 5 is not a cross-type mathematical conversion. Build the expected BigInteger explicitly and compare it with the returned BigInteger value.

assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(5),
    BigNumbers.addOne(BigInteger.valueOf(4)));

flow.title: Write a complete test without a skeleton
flow.html:
You have chosen inputs, constructed values, selected assertions, and repaired test structure separately. Now write one complete test with those pieces. Keep the goal small: a rejected Counter update must throw and preserve its prior value. The prompt gives the full contract; your job is to express that one behavior accurately.

Decide the fixture, the rejected action, and the two observations before writing the method.

flow.title: Explain the evidence without overclaiming
flow.html:
A test is useful when you can explain what it checks and what it leaves open. A pass says the executed assertions held for that run. It does not repair a wrong oracle, prove untested boundaries, or guarantee coverage of unseen branches. Clear limits help you choose the next useful case instead of relying on a green indicator alone.

Name the checked contract clause, the concrete input, and any separate obligation still needing evidence.

int[] actual = ArrayCopies.copy(input);

A non-null empty input and its result are stored in int[] input and int[] actual. Which assertion directly checks the required different-array identity?

Write void modifyingCopyKeepsInput(). Use input new int[]{4, 9}, copy it, change the copied first element to 99, then verify the original first element is still 4.

@Test
void modifyingCopyKeepsInput() {

    int[] actual = ArrayCopies.copy(input);

Calls ArrayCopies.copy and stores its result.
Mutates actual[0], not input[0].

practice.title: Read the implementation’s alias defect
practice.prompt:
static int[] ArrayCopies.copy(int[] values) accepts a non-null int array and returns a different array containing the same ints in the same order. The arrays must be independent, including when empty. It leaves input unchanged. Null throws NullPointerException; no message is specified.

A faulty implementation rejects null correctly, then executes return values;. For input {4, 9}, the caller sets the returned array’s element 0 to 99. Explain expected versus actual original element 0, and the cause.
practice.hint: Returning values copies a reference, not the int elements into another array.
practice.solution: The original element 0 should remain 4, but it becomes 99. Returning values makes result and input aliases of one array, so the result mutation changes the original storage. Equal-content assertions at return time alone would miss this defect.

Connects return values to shared array identity.
Explains why content equality alone can pass.

practice.prompt:
static int[] ArrayCopies.copy(int[] values) accepts a non-null int array and returns a different array containing the same ints in the same order. The arrays must be independent, including when empty. It leaves input unchanged. Null throws NullPointerException; no message is specified.

new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

A valid Counter counter is already created. Repair this statement into the two correct statements for storing and checking 5. Explain why the original does not compile.

counter.set(5);
assertEquals(5, counter.get());

practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

The following is the entire test body after valid Counter setup. A defective set(-1) returns normally. Which repair makes that missing exception fail the test?

practice.title: Write a complete test without a skeleton
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts at 0. int get() returns its value. void set(int next) stores a nonnegative value; a negative value must throw IllegalArgumentException with message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the old value unchanged.

Assume the Jupiter @Test and assertion imports are present. Write the method inside an ordinary test class.

Independently write void rejectionPreservesPreviousValue(). Start with value 7, attempt -2, use assertThrows for the promised exception, then verify value 7 remains. A message assertion is optional because this task focuses on type and state.

@Test
void rejectionPreservesPreviousValue() {
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    counter.set(7);
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
        () -> counter.set(-2));
    assertEquals(7, counter.get());
}

Creates a fresh Counter and arranges value 7 before the checked action.
